spec_match.rationale: Every interface member is read from the browser's own prototypes, getDevices is called for real, and requestDevice is called for real in both directions — with and without a gesture. The platform is read from user-agent client hints rather than parsed from the UA string, with the string included as a foil to be measured against.

interactive.rationale: A live interface reader with a getDevices poll; a platform panel with a high-entropy hint request behind a button; and a filter builder that renders the exact call and then makes it, from a click and from a timer.

blurb_alignment.rationale: The index says the feature removes an arbitrary boundary rather than adding a capability, names the devices that motivate it, and states up front that the Android behaviour could not be tested from a desktop.

edge_cases.rationale: The empty getDevices result, which is the normal answer and not a capability check; the closed chooser, which resolves with an empty array rather than rejecting; the missing gesture, demonstrated rather than described; and permissions.query({name:'hid'}) rejecting with a TypeError, which means a page cannot ask about its standing in advance.

references.rationale: chromestatus.com/feature/5172464636133376 on the index and all three concept pages, with the WebHID specification, MDN, the USB-IF usage tables and the client hints specification.

conformance.rationale: Six immutable assertions: navigator.hid exists; both entry points exist; HIDDevice carries the full report surface; getDevices needs no gesture and returns an array; requestDevice without a gesture rejects with SecurityError or NotAllowedError; and the platform is readable separately from the capability.

runtime_evidence.rationale: deno task drive over all three pages in real Chrome 150: 3/3, 24 assertions. Verified: the full HID and HIDDevice member lists, getDevices returning an empty array without a gesture, permissions.query({name:'hid'}) rejecting with TypeError, the platform reading Linux / not-mobile / formFactors ['Desktop'], and requestDevice from a timer rejecting with the exact SecurityError. NOT verified: anything about Android, and anything involving a real device — the machine is a desktop with no HID device permitted, and the feature is precisely about the platform this is not.

telemetry_health.rationale: Each page emits showcaseTelemetry.assert with the device count, the platform readings and the outcome of each requestDevice attempt.

design_system.rationale: CSS variables throughout, no raw colour literals, buttons set background and colour, 44px control minimums, and the wide tables in their own scroll containers.

accessibility.rationale: The journal is role=log with a name; every verdict is a sentence; the platform table names its source per row so a screen reader gets the provenance with the value; results are announced through aria-live.

mobile_desktop_parity.rationale: Control grids are auto-fit minmax and stack at 360px; the member chip lists wrap; every table scrolls in its own container. Mobile is the class this feature is about, and the pages are built to be read on one.

openQuestions.title: The feature itself is untested, and cannot be tested from here
openQuestions.detail: Everything measured on this machine is the desktop behaviour, which has been available since Chrome 89. Whether a specialised HID device works on Android needs an Android device with a device attached — and would exercise the same three pages unchanged, since none of them hard-codes a platform. Until then the runtime evidence is honestly partial and the platform page says so in the table itself.

openQuestions.title: No page reads a report
openQuestions.detail: The interesting half of WebHID is what arrives on inputreport — a headset's mute button, a keypad's custom layout — and no page here shows one, because no device is permitted. A fourth concept that opens a permitted device and renders its report bytes would be the natural next step, and needs hardware rather than more code.

guidanceConsulted.query: announce the result of a permission-gated call in a live region
guidanceConsulted.recommendation: State what was attempted and what happened, including the rejection, rather than leaving the user with an unchanged screen.
guidanceConsulted.appliedOrException: Every call is journalled with its arguments and outcome in a role=log element, and the narrative result — including the exact SecurityError message and what it means — is written into an aria-live output.
guidanceConsulted.evidence: deno task drive asserts both the journal entry and the explanation text after a scripted call.

guidanceConsulted.query: accessible controls that build a call from parts
guidanceConsulted.recommendation: Label every control, show the resulting value as it changes, and keep presets and manual entry consistent with each other.
guidanceConsulted.appliedOrException: The filter builder renders the exact call on every input, and choosing a preset writes into the same fields rather than bypassing them — so the reader can always see what the preset did.
guidanceConsulted.evidence: deno task drive selects a preset and asserts the rendered call changed accordingly.

guidanceConsulted.query: responsive tables and chip lists without horizontal overflow
guidanceConsulted.recommendation: Auto-fit control grids; wide tables in their own scroll container; let chip lists wrap.
guidanceConsulted.evidence: responsive-check desktop + mobile on the feature.

summary: Three concepts about a platform boundary being removed, built on a machine on the wrong side of it. Everything reachable is measured — the full interface, the empty permitted-device list, the unqueryable permission name, and the exact gesture rejection — and the pages keep the capability question, the platform question and the permission question visibly separate, which is the mistake the feature invites.
